metadata.title: A short proof of Cauchy's polygonal number theorem

extraction_notes.note: Mathpix source: no environments or labels; equations (1)-(6) are \tag'd unnumbered displays not reported as facts, so they were added by hand as equation nodes. A \footnotetext (editorial dates, MSC codes) sits inside the proof of Cauchy's Lemma and is therefore part of PP2's verbatim statement.
theorem (external) or not a node: Pepin's tables are a cited computational result, kept because the reduction PP1 to $n \geqslant 120m$ relies on it.

'In both cases, the theorem follows immediately from Cauchy's Lemma' is both a reunion sentence (step rule 8: its own conclusion step) and an immediate sentence (step rule 6); the finishing step enforces rule 6, so it is appended to the last case step.
Cauchy's Lemma and Cauchy's theorem are attributed to Cauchy and only re-proved here, so marked external although the paper's main contribution is their short proof (PP1, PP2, Theorem 1).

nodes.name: polygonal numbers of order m+2
nodes.statement: Let $m \geqslant 1$. The polygonal numbers of order $m+2$ are the integers $$ p_{m}(k)=\frac{m}{2}\left(k^{2}-k\right)+k $$ for $k=0,1,2, \ldots$.
nodes.statement_short: The polygonal numbers of order $m+2$ are $p_m(k)=\frac{m}{2}(k^2-k)+k$ for $k\ge 0$.

nodes.name: Cauchy's polygonal number theorem
nodes.statement: Fermat [3] asserted that every nonnegative integer is the sum of $m+2$ polygonal numbers of order $m+2$.
conclusions: every nonnegative integer is the sum of $m+2$ polygonal numbers of order $m+2$
nodes.statement_short: Fermat's assertion (proved by Cauchy): every $n\ge 0$ is a sum of $m+2$ polygonal numbers of order $m+2$.

nodes.name: Lagrange's four-square theorem
nodes.statement: For $m=2$, Lagrange [5] proved that every nonnegative integer is the sum of four squares $p_{2}(k)=k^{2}$.
conclusions: every nonnegative integer is the sum of four squares $p_{2}(k)=k^{2}$

nodes.name: Gauss's triangular number theorem
nodes.statement: For $m=1$, Gauss [4] proved that every nonnegative integer is the sum of three triangular numbers $p_{1}(k)=\left(k^{2}+k\right) / 2$, or, equivalently, that every positive integer $n \equiv 3(\bmod 8)$ is the sum of three odd squares.
conclusions: every nonnegative integer is the sum of three triangular numbers $p_{1}(k)=\left(k^{2}+k\right) / 2$
every positive integer $n \equiv 3(\bmod 8)$ is the sum of three odd squares
nodes.statement_short: Every $n\ge0$ is a sum of three triangular numbers; equivalently every $n\equiv 3 \pmod 8$ is a sum of three odd squares.

nodes.name: Pepin's tables
nodes.statement: For $m \geqslant 3$ and $n \leqslant 120 m$, Pepin [8] published tables of explicit representations of $n$ as a sum of $m+2$ polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, at most four of which are different from 0 or 1.
conclusions: explicit representations of $n$ as a sum of $m+2$ polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, at most four of which are different from 0 or 1
nodes.statement_short: Pepin tabulated explicit representations of all $n\le 120m$ as sums of $m+2$ polygonal numbers, at most four not 0 or 1.

nodes.name: Reduction of Cauchy's theorem to $n \geqslant 120m$
nodes.statement: Because of Pepin's and Dickson's tables, it suffices to consider only $n \geqslant 120 m$.
nodes.statement_short: Pepin's and Dickson's tables cover $n\le 120m$, so Theorem 1 for $n\ge 120m$ suffices.

nodes.name: Cauchy's Lemma
nodes.statement: Cauchy's Lemma. Let $a$ and $b$ be odd positive integers such that $b^{2}<4 a$ and $3 a<b^{2}+2 b+4$. Then there exist nonnegative integers $s, t, u, v$ such that \begin{align*} & a=s^{2}+t^{2}+u^{2}+v^{2} \tag{1}\\ & b=s+t+u+v \tag{2} \end{align*}
assumptions: $a$ and $b$ be odd positive integers such that $b^{2}<4 a$ and $3 a<b^{2}+2 b+4$
conclusions: there exist nonnegative integers $s, t, u, v$ such that
nodes.statement_short: If $a,b$ odd with $b^2<4a$ and $3a<b^2+2b+4$, then $a$ is a sum of four squares $s^2+\dots+v^2$ with $s+t+u+v=b$, all $\ge 0$.

nodes.name: Sum of the four integers (2)
nodes.statement: & b=s+t+u+v \tag{2}

nodes.name: Proof of Cauchy's Lemma
nodes.statement: Proof. Since $a$ and $b$ are odd, it follows that $4 a-b^{2} \equiv 3(\bmod 8)$, and so, by Gauss's triangular number theorem, there exist odd integers $x \geqslant y \geqslant z>0$ such that \begin{equation*} 4 a-b^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} . \tag{3} \end{equation*} \footnotetext{Received by the editors August 26, 1985 and, in revised form, December 20, 1985.\\ 1980 Mathematics Subject Classification (1985 Revision). Primary 11P05, 11B83, 11B13.\\ Key words and phrases. Polygonal numbers, sums of squares, Cauchy-Fermat theorem. }Choose the sign of $\pm z$ so that $b+x+y \pm z \equiv 0(\bmod 4)$. Define integers $s, t, u, v$ by $$ \begin{gathered} s=\frac{b+x+y \pm z}{4}, \quad t=\frac{b+x}{2}-s=\frac{b+x-y \mp z}{4}, \\ u=\frac{b+y}{2}-s=\frac{b-x+y \mp z}{4}, \quad v=\frac{b \pm z}{2}-s=\frac{b-x-y \pm z}{4} . \end{gathered} $$ Then equations (1) and (2) are satisfied, and $s \geqslant t \geqslant u \geqslant v$. To show these integers are nonnegative, it suffices to prove that $v \geqslant 0$, or $v>-1$. This is true if $b-x-y$ $-z>-4$, or, equivalently, if $x+y+z<b+4$. The maximum value of $x+y+z$ subject to the constraint (3) is $\sqrt{12 a-3 b^{2}}$, and the inequality $3 a<b^{2}+2 b+4$ implies that $x+y+z \leqslant \sqrt{12 a-3 b^{2}}<b+4$. This proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Gauss's three-odd-squares theorem to $4a-b^2$, define $s,t,u,v$ linearly from $x,y,z,b$. Nonnegativity follows from $x+y+z\le\sqrt{12a-3b^2}<b+4$.

nodes.name: Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Theorem 1. Let $m \geqslant 3$ and $n \geqslant 120 m$. Then $n$ is the sum of $m+1$ polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, at most four of which are different from 0 or 1.
conclusions: $n$ is the sum of $m+1$ polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, at most four of which are different from 0 or 1
nodes.statement_short: For $m\ge3$, every $n\ge 120m$ is a sum of $m+1$ polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, at most four not 0 or 1.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Proof. Let $b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$ be consecutive odd integers. The set of numbers of the form $b+r$, where $b \in\left\{b_{1}, b_{2}\right\}$ and $r \in\{0,1, \ldots, m-3\}$, contains a complete set of residue classes modulo $m$, and so $n \equiv b+r(\bmod m)$ for some $b \in\left\{b_{1}, b_{2}\right\}$ and $r \in\{0,1, \ldots, m-3\}$. Define \begin{equation*} a=2\left(\frac{n-b-r}{m}\right)+b=\left(1-\frac{2}{m}\right) b+2\left(\frac{n-r}{m}\right) . \tag{4} \end{equation*} Then $a$ is an odd integer, and \begin{equation*} n=\frac{m}{2}(a-b)+b+r . \tag{5} \end{equation*} If $0<b<\frac{2}{3}+\sqrt{8(n / m)-8}$, then the quadratic formula implies that $$ b^{2}-4 a=b^{2}-4\left(1-\frac{2}{m}\right) b-8\left(\frac{n-r}{m}\right)<0 $$ and so $b^{2}<4 a$. Similarly, if $b>\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{6(n / m)-3}$, then $3 a<b^{2}+2 b+4$. Since the length of the interval \begin{equation*} I=\left(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{6\left(\frac{n}{m}\right)-3}, \frac{2}{3}+\sqrt{8\left(\frac{n}{m}\right)-8}\right) \tag{6} \end{equation*} is greater than 4, it follows that $I$ contains two consecutive odd positive integers $b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$. Thus, there exist odd positive integers $a$ and $b$ that satisfy (5) and the inequalities $b^{2}<4 a$ and $3 a<b^{2}+2 b+4$. Cauchy's Lemma implies that there exist $s, t, u, v$ satisfying (1) and (2), and so $$ \begin{aligned} n & =\frac{m}{2}(a-b)+b+r=\frac{m}{2}\left(s^{2}-s\right)+s+\cdots+\frac{m}{2}\left(v^{2}-v\right)+v+r \\ & =p_{m}(s)+p_{m}(t)+p_{m}(u)+p_{m}(v)+r . \end{aligned} $$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Choose odd $b$ and $r\le m-3$ with $n\equiv b+r \pmod m$ and $b$ in an interval of length $>4$ making Cauchy's Lemma applicable; then $n=\sum p_m(\cdot)+r$.

nodes.name: Definition of a (4)
nodes.statement: a=2\left(\frac{n-b-r}{m}\right)+b=\left(1-\frac{2}{m}\right) b+2\left(\frac{n-r}{m}\right) . \tag{4}

nodes.name: Representation of n (5)
nodes.statement: n=\frac{m}{2}(a-b)+b+r . \tag{5}

nodes.name: Interval I (6)
nodes.statement: I=\left(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{6\left(\frac{n}{m}\right)-3}, \frac{2}{3}+\sqrt{8\left(\frac{n}{m}\right)-8}\right) \tag{6}

nodes.name: Theorem 1 is stronger than Cauchy's theorem
nodes.statement: Note that this result is slightly stronger than Cauchy's theorem.

nodes.name: Legendre's theorem on five polygonal numbers
nodes.statement: Legendre [6] proved that every sufficiently large integer is the sum of five polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, one of which is either 0 or 1.
conclusions: every sufficiently large integer is the sum of five polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, one of which is either 0 or 1

nodes.name: Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Theorem 2. Let $m \geqslant 3$. If $m$ is odd, then every sufficiently large integer is the sum of four polygonal numbers of order $m+2$. If $m$ is even, then every sufficiently large integer is the sum of five polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, one of which is either 0 or 1.
conclusions: every sufficiently large integer is the sum of four polygonal numbers of order $m+2$
every sufficiently large integer is the sum of five polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, one of which is either 0 or 1
every sufficiently large integer is the sum of four polygonal numbers of order $m+2$
every sufficiently large integer is the sum of five polygonal numbers of order $m+2$, one of which is either 0 or 1

nodes.statement_short: For $m\ge3$, large integers are sums of four (m odd) or five, one of them 0 or 1 (m even), polygonal numbers of order $m+2$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Proof. There is an absolute constant $c$ such that if $n>c m^{3}$, then the length of the interval $I$ defined in (6) is greater than $2 m$, and so $I$ contains at least $m$ consecutive odd integers. If $m$ is odd, these form a complete set of residues modulo $m$, and so $n \equiv b$ $(\bmod m)$ for some odd number $b \in I$. Let $r=0$. Define $a$ by formula (4). If $m$ is even and $n>c m^{3}$, then $n \equiv b+r(\bmod m)$ for some odd integer $b \in I$ and $r \in\{0,1\}$. Define $a$ by (4). In both cases, the theorem follows immediately from Cauchy's Lemma.
nodes.statement_short: For $n>cm^3$ the interval $I$ holds $m$ consecutive odd integers, so residues mod $m$ are hit with $r=0$ (m odd) or $r\in\{0,1\}$ (m even); apply Cauchy's Lemma.

nodes.name: Apply Gauss's theorem
nodes.statement: Since $a$ and $b$ are odd, it follows that $4 a-b^{2} \equiv 3(\bmod 8)$, and so, by Gauss's triangular number theorem, there exist odd integers $x \geqslant y \geqslant z>0$ such that \begin{equation*} 4 a-b^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} . \tag{3} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Gauss's triangular number theorem to $4a-b^2\equiv 3\pmod 8$.

nodes.name: Define s, t, u, v
nodes.statement: Choose the sign of $\pm z$ so that $b+x+y \pm z \equiv 0(\bmod 4)$. Define integers $s, t, u, v$ by $$ \begin{gathered} s=\frac{b+x+y \pm z}{4}, \quad t=\frac{b+x}{2}-s=\frac{b+x-y \mp z}{4}, \\ u=\frac{b+y}{2}-s=\frac{b-x+y \mp z}{4}, \quad v=\frac{b \pm z}{2}-s=\frac{b-x-y \pm z}{4} . \end{gathered} $$
nodes.statement_short: Choose the sign of $z$ and define $s,t,u,v$.

nodes.name: Verify (1), (2) and ordering
nodes.statement: Then equations (1) and (2) are satisfied, and $s \geqslant t \geqslant u \geqslant v$.
nodes.statement_short: Check that $s,t,u,v$ satisfy (1), (2) and are ordered.

nodes.name: Reduce nonnegativity to x+y+z<b+4
nodes.statement: To show these integers are nonnegative, it suffices to prove that $v \geqslant 0$, or $v>-1$. This is true if $b-x-y$ $-z>-4$, or, equivalently, if $x+y+z<b+4$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce nonnegativity to $x+y+z<b+4$.

nodes.name: Bound x+y+z
nodes.statement: The maximum value of $x+y+z$ subject to the constraint (3) is $\sqrt{12 a-3 b^{2}}$, and the inequality $3 a<b^{2}+2 b+4$ implies that $x+y+z \leqslant \sqrt{12 a-3 b^{2}}<b+4$. This proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $x+y+z\le\sqrt{12a-3b^2}<b+4$ and conclude.

nodes.name: Choose residues b + r
nodes.statement: Let $b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$ be consecutive odd integers. The set of numbers of the form $b+r$, where $b \in\left\{b_{1}, b_{2}\right\}$ and $r \in\{0,1, \ldots, m-3\}$, contains a complete set of residue classes modulo $m$, and so $n \equiv b+r(\bmod m)$ for some $b \in\left\{b_{1}, b_{2}\right\}$ and $r \in\{0,1, \ldots, m-3\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take consecutive odd $b_1,b_2$; some $b+r$ with $r\le m-3$ is $\equiv n \pmod m$.

nodes.name: Define a
nodes.statement: Define \begin{equation*} a=2\left(\frac{n-b-r}{m}\right)+b=\left(1-\frac{2}{m}\right) b+2\left(\frac{n-r}{m}\right) . \tag{4} \end{equation*} Then $a$ is an odd integer, and \begin{equation*} n=\frac{m}{2}(a-b)+b+r . \tag{5} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Define $a$ by (4); it is odd and gives (5).

nodes.name: Inequalities on b
nodes.statement: If $0<b<\frac{2}{3}+\sqrt{8(n / m)-8}$, then the quadratic formula implies that $$ b^{2}-4 a=b^{2}-4\left(1-\frac{2}{m}\right) b-8\left(\frac{n-r}{m}\right)<0 $$ and so $b^{2}<4 a$. Similarly, if $b>\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{6(n / m)-3}$, then $3 a<b^{2}+2 b+4$.
nodes.statement_short: Via the quadratic formula, $b$ in the given range gives $b^2<4a$ and $3a<b^2+2b+4$.

nodes.name: Interval I contains b1, b2
nodes.statement: Since the length of the interval \begin{equation*} I=\left(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{6\left(\frac{n}{m}\right)-3}, \frac{2}{3}+\sqrt{8\left(\frac{n}{m}\right)-8}\right) \tag{6} \end{equation*} is greater than 4, it follows that $I$ contains two consecutive odd positive integers $b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$. Thus, there exist odd positive integers $a$ and $b$ that satisfy (5) and the inequalities $b^{2}<4 a$ and $3 a<b^{2}+2 b+4$.
nodes.statement_short: The interval $I$ has length $>4$, so suitable odd $a,b$ exist.

nodes.name: Apply Cauchy's Lemma
nodes.statement: Cauchy's Lemma implies that there exist $s, t, u, v$ satisfying (1) and (2), and so $$ \begin{aligned} n & =\frac{m}{2}(a-b)+b+r=\frac{m}{2}\left(s^{2}-s\right)+s+\cdots+\frac{m}{2}\left(v^{2}-v\right)+v+r \\ & =p_{m}(s)+p_{m}(t)+p_{m}(u)+p_{m}(v)+r . \end{aligned} $$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Cauchy's Lemma and rewrite $n$ as a sum of polygonal numbers plus $r$.

nodes.name: Interval I is long
nodes.statement: There is an absolute constant $c$ such that if $n>c m^{3}$, then the length of the interval $I$ defined in (6) is greater than $2 m$, and so $I$ contains at least $m$ consecutive odd integers.
nodes.statement_short: For $n>cm^3$, $I$ has length $>2m$ and holds $m$ consecutive odd integers.

nodes.name: Case m odd
nodes.statement: If $m$ is odd, these form a complete set of residues modulo $m$, and so $n \equiv b$ $(\bmod m)$ for some odd number $b \in I$. Let $r=0$. Define $a$ by formula (4).
nodes.statement_short: Odd $m$: hit residue with $b$ alone, $r=0$.

nodes.name: Case m even; conclude
nodes.statement: If $m$ is even and $n>c m^{3}$, then $n \equiv b+r(\bmod m)$ for some odd integer $b \in I$ and $r \in\{0,1\}$. Define $a$ by (4). In both cases, the theorem follows immediately from Cauchy's Lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Even $m$: hit residue with $b+r$, $r\in\{0,1\}$; both cases then follow from Cauchy's Lemma.
